 Nicholas Wu and Burgess Everett Nov 20, 2026, 5:30am EST Politics Share Liesa Johannssen/Reuters; Evelyn Hockstein/Reuters Post Email Whatsapp Copy link Sign up for Semafor Washington, DC: What the White House is reading. Read it now .

 Notable
 The News
 Chuck Schumer and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are steering clear of each other for now — yet their political futures are increasingly entangled.
 As the Senate Democratic leader battles an underdog leadership challenge from Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., some of his members are hoping for signals about his reelection plans for 2028. If Schumer seeks another six-year term, progressives are agitating for a primary challenge.
 And if Ocasio-Cortez passes on a White House run, many on the left want her in the Senate. Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., said the 37-year-old should challenge Schumer, 75, “if she’s not running for president.”
 Ocasio-Cortez is keeping fellow Democrats guessing about her plans. While allies like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed are backing Van Hollen, she also appears to be staying out of Schumer’s leadership race. Ocasio-Cortez told Semafor in a brief interview that his future as majority leader is “for the other chamber to determine.”
 AD 
 Schumer is similarly mum on 2028, even when talking with Democratic senators. He views winning the majority leader job and a future reelection bid as separate choices, with the former having no bearing on the latter, according to a person familiar with his thinking.
 His decision has an undeniable effect on her options, however. Ocasio-Cortez would likely clear the field in an open primary to succeed Schumer, the only septuagenarian among the top four Hill leaders. Schumer also has good reason, despite Van Hollen’s challenge, to take his time deciding after helping his party flip a historic nine Senate seats this year.
 Ocasio-Cortez may choose a primary fight for higher office, according to several House Democrats. She made her name eight years ago by dethroning Joe Crowley, a former member of House leadership, and she would be a formidable statewide candidate regardless of Schumer’s decision.
 AD 
 “I’m sure she’s thinking about it. I’m not sure she’s thinking about it in the context of what Chuck does,” said Rep. Joe Morelle, D-N.Y. “She’s probably just trying to make a decision on what she thinks she can best contribute.”
 Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., predicted that “there will be” a primary bid, adding that Ocasio-Cortez “has so many options in front of her.”
 Schumer’s plans 
 Schumer hasn’t tipped his hand to even close allies in the caucus about running for another term. He is the heavy favorite to defeat Van Hollen but taking the battle seriously.
 AD 
 Still, sharing his views on 2028 could “obviously” help him more handily defeat the Marylander, one Democratic senator told Semafor.
 “I don’t think Leader Schumer needs to make some public pronouncement about his future plans, but I think it is helpful for us as a caucus to be thinking about what kind of leadership team and what kind of leader we want in this moment for the next two years — and going forward,” this senator said. “Because they may not be the same.”
 The question of Schumer’s future is complex: He is singularly focused on leading Democrats through the last two years of President Donald Trump’s term, but it’s also rare for Senate leaders to run again after facing dissent within their own ranks.
 Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi took her own version of that step in 2022 by announcing she would leave leadership so incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries could rise, though she served another two-year term. Schumer won the Democratic leader job in one day after former Leader Harry Reid announced his retirement and backed Schumer in 2015.
 Most Democrats speculate, without direct knowledge, that Schumer is leaning against another Senate term.
 If Ocasio-Cortez ran for president or stayed in the House, Schumer could potentially survive a primary challenge from another opponent. The crowded bench of candidates who might jump into an open primary includes Rep. Pat Ryan, D-N.Y., whom Democrats have long considered a potential statewide candidate.
 Ryan doesn’t sound eager to challenge Schumer head-on yet. He told Semafor that Schumer “deserves a tremendous amount of credit for those wins, for putting us in the position we’re in, and then it’s his decision to do whatever he wants to do next.” The 44-year-old added that he didn’t want to get ahead of “what [Schumer] wants to do.” Whether Schumer should be majority leader was “up to the Senate side,” he said.
 ‘How to yield power’ 
 Senators generally are not influenced by House members’ opinions on their internal matters or politics. But indicating that he’s not running could affect Schumer’s ability to lead the caucus over the next two years, some Democrats said.
 “That’s the kind of calculation that he has to figure out for himself,” said Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who supports Schumer. “And also, what does that mean for actually holding power, how to yield power — does it help you use influence? So, those are the kind of decisions that he has to make.”
 El-Sayed, who defeated a Schumer-backed primary foe in Michigan, did not seem interested in fueling a primary challenge to the leader. In an interview, El-Sayed said he has “nothing against Senator Schumer. It’s not about him.”
 “The most important priority for us right now is that we have to have a plan to legislate in ways that the American public can understand, identifying their problems, identifying legislation that’s going to solve their problems, and then executing on that,” El-Sayed added.

 If Schumer did indicate to his caucus that he won’t seek reelection, he’d be sharing more than most Democratic senators do. None of the ambitious Democrats he leads have said explicitly yet that they are running for president, for all their visits to early states and ambitious agendas.
 “The more information, the better,” said Sen. Ben Ray Lujan, D-N.M., who is neutral in the leadership race. “But I’ve not experienced colleagues ever telling us what they’re doing in a week, much less over the next few years.”
 Burgess’s view
 It’s clear that some progressives want Ocasio-Cortez to run for Senate rather than president. For all her name recognition, she would face a White House primary that promises to be as brutal as 2020’s 29-candidate field.
 But as she indicates she’ll decide at her own speed — she’s one of the few 2028 contenders with the luxury of doing so — we see the pragmatic side of Ocasio-Cortez.
 She’s tamped down progressive criticism of Jeffries. Her answer on Van Hollen was in the same vein. She’s deliberate before choosing to roil her party.
 Notable
 When Ocasio-Cortez and El-Sayed campaigned together in Michigan’s rural Upper Peninsula this fall, they were clearly test-driving a national platform for the left, as Semafor reported .
